main.summary: Demoted to Huangzhou, Wang Yucheng builds a small bamboo tower at the north-west corner of the town and describes the quiet pleasures of listening to rain, reading the Book of Changes and enjoying the view. He ends with a sigh about the shifting course of an official career and hopes that those who come later will keep repairing the tower.
main.translation:
The land around Huanggang has a great deal of bamboo, and the big stalks are as thick as rafters. The bamboo workers split them, hollow out the joints, and use them in place of pottery tiles. Every house is roofed like this, because it is cheap and saves labour.
At the north-west corner of the inner town, the battlements had collapsed and the place was overgrown with weeds and rubbish, so I built a small tower of two bays there, joined to the Moonwave Tower. In the distance it swallows the colour of the hills; level with the eye it scoops up the rapids of the river. It is secluded, silent and wide-reaching, and cannot be fully described.
In summer it suits a sudden shower, with a sound like a waterfall; in winter it suits dense snow, with a sound like broken jade. It suits playing the zither, for the tune is hollow and free; it suits chanting poems, for the rhymes are pure and fine; it suits playing weiqi, for the stones make a tinkling sound; it suits pitch-pot, for the arrows ring clear. All of these are helped by the bamboo tower.
In the time off after official duty, I put on a crane-feather coat and wear a Huayang cap, and holding a volume of the Book of Changes I burn incense and sit in silence, dispelling the cares of the world. Beyond the river and hills I see only wind-filled sails and sandbirds, mist, clouds, bamboo and trees. When the strength of the wine has worn off and the tea smoke has died away, I see off the setting sun and welcome the pale moon; this too is one of the fine things about a life in exile.
Those towers, Qiyun and Luoxing, are high indeed; Jinggan and Licao are splendid indeed; but they only serve to keep singing girls and hide song and dance, and they are not the business of poets, so I do not take them as a model.
I have heard the bamboo workers say: 'Bamboo used as tiles lasts barely ten years; if it is laid in a double layer, twenty.' Ah! In the year yiwei of Zhidao I was sent from the Hanlin Academy to Chuzhou; in bingshen I was moved to Guangling; in dingyou I returned to the western chancellery; on the last day of the year wuxu, I received the order for Qi'an; and in the intercalary third month of jihai I reached the prefecture. In four years I have had no time to rest from running about, and I do not know where I shall be next year. Why should I fear that the bamboo tower rots easily? I hope that those who come after will share my purpose, take it up and repair it, so that this tower may not perish. Written on the fifteenth day of the eighth month of the second year of Xianping.

keyLines.line: 夏宜急雨，有瀑布聲；冬宜密雪，有碎玉聲
keyLines.en: In summer it suits a sudden shower, with a sound like a waterfall; in winter it suits dense snow, with a sound like broken jade.
keyLines.note: He writes the pleasures of the seasons through sound: rain like a waterfall, snow like jade, to show the clear and ringing quality of the bamboo tower.

keyLines.line: 公退之暇，被鶴氅衣，戴華陽巾，手執《周易》一卷，焚香默坐，消遣世慮
keyLines.en: In the time off after official duty, I put on a crane-feather coat and wear a Huayang cap, and holding a volume of the Book of Changes I burn incense and sit in silence, dispelling the cares of the world.
keyLines.note: He describes his dress and quiet days; reading the Changes and sitting still show an easy, content spirit after his demotion.

keyLines.line: 送夕陽，迎素月，亦謫居之勝槩也
keyLines.en: I see off the setting sun and welcome the pale moon; this too is one of the fine things about a life in exile.
keyLines.note: Finding contentment in exile; this is the turning point and heart of the whole piece.

keyLines.line: 止於貯妓女，藏歌舞，非騷人之事，吾所不取
keyLines.en: But they only serve to keep singing girls and hide song and dance, and they are not the business of poets, so I do not take them as a model.
keyLines.note: By putting down extravagant towers, he shows that his own taste is for what is simple and refined.

keyLines.line: 未知明年又在何處，豈懼竹樓之易朽乎
keyLines.en: I do not know where I shall be next year. Why should I fear that the bamboo tower rots easily?
keyLines.note: From the tower's quick decay he turns to a sigh about the ups and downs of an official life, open-minded but touched with helplessness.

keyLines.line: 幸後之人，與我同志，嗣而葺之，庶斯樓之不朽也
keyLines.en: I hope that those who come after will share my purpose, take it up and repair it, so that this tower may not perish.
keyLines.note: He hopes later people will carry on his purpose, so that the tower and the spirit it stands for will last together.

glossary.note: A small walled town inside the large city, usually where the government offices were.
The low wall along the top of a city wall, the parapet.
A tower on the wall of Huangzhou, joined to the bamboo tower.
A coat made of bird feathers, worn by Daoists or hermits.
A head-cloth worn by Daoist recluses.
An ancient game at banquets in which arrows are thrown into a pot, and the winner is decided by the number that go in.
A poet or man of letters; the term comes from Qu Yuan's Lisao.
Another name for the Secretariat; here it means the post of drafter in the Secretariat.

main.background: Wang Yucheng (954-1001) was a poet and prose writer of the early Northern Song (960-1127) who was demoted several times for speaking frankly. He wrote this piece in 999 while serving as prefect at Huangzhou. It belongs to the 'ji' (record) form, with a plain, fresh style, and it is one of the works that stood against the showy fashion of the early Song.
